searchText: Hi everybody, hope you don't mind me posting here. I'm looking at the recent EOF presentation slides from ACDE. I'm interested in the argument that immediate values change the interpretation of existing code. The example given (slides 23/24) is: `0x61E001615B610100EFE05BFFC92A` The argument is that adding `RJUMP` leads to a change in validity of the code. But, I don't see that (in this particular case) it is true. Assembly code for the example is: ``` .code push 0xe001 push 0x5b61 add stop .data 0xefe05bffc92a ``` My understanding of the Yellow Paper suggests that this code would not be affected by the introduction of `RJUMP` as it does not attempt a branch to the second `JUMPDEST`. Hence, whether or not its considered a valid Jump Destination does not matter. *Did I miss something here?* Anyway, an example like this seems to make more sense to me: ``` .code push lab jump db 0xe0 lab: jumpdest stop ``` In this case, reinterpreting `0xe0` as an `RJUMP` with a two-byte immediate operand completely changes the meaning of the program. It's not the best example, mostly to illustrate the overwrite, and an incomplete segment. Its still allowed by legacy rules, so we also need to be bould by what is possible and not what is logical. Which ASM are you using and what is the db symbol for? The assembly language is just made up for the example based on other assembly languages (see e.g [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/22554838)). `db` stands for databyte and is a common way to indicate a raw byte. `dw` is also typically used for a data word, etc. So, my next question then. I'm not super familiar with the inner working of the Solidity or Vyper compilers. But, do we have any reasons to expect arbitrary bytes within a contract's bytecode, other than as a single block at the very end? For example, compilers might in theory insert constants at arbitrary positions in the code, etc. We need to worry about what is possible, not what Vyper and Solidity does. Voluntarily following conventions does make it easier, but it is still possible to do non-conventional things all EVMs must support. Solidity does currently re-write contracts to handle immutable constants initialized in the constructor. That's why we need data sections and DATALOADN addresses the size regression. > We need to worry about what is possible, not what Vyper and Solidity does. Yeah, I understand. I'm just trying to get a feel for the current state of play. > Solidity does currently re-write contracts to handle immutable constants initialized in the constructor. I'm not following what you're getting at here. Does it result in constant bytes at arbitrary positions in the bytecode? > That's why we need data sections Yeah, I understand the benefit of splitting out code from data. It makes complete sense to me to do it like this. I think that's what they do. The contained bytecode in initcode would contain blank data or be done in parts and then either replaced or copied in sections. But per their docs it's a code alteration, not just a data section reference. > But per their docs it's a code alteration, not just a data section reference. Yeah, ok I understand ... you're talking about treating contract code as a template before deployment with `CREATE`, etc. But I'm interested more in this argument around immediate operands. Adding immediates to the legacy EVM won't pass security researcher scrutny. Ok ... but if you can make the argument that its _impossible_ to add to the legacy EVM .... then the EOF case is stronger, no ? Whilst the _possibility_ remains that immediates could be added to the legacy EVM ... then seems to me its a harder sell I'm just trying to understand if its really impossible or not It's been tried and rejected. Sure, but its still an argument someone can make. If you can say: *no its actually impossible to do this and here's why*. Then, there's no argument. Nothing is truely impossible in the EVM. It's a question of how much breakage you are willing to introduce. Historically the amount of breakage immediates add was higher than was acceptable. The appetite for breakage as decreased, not increased. > It's a question of how much breakage you are willing to introduce. Right. And I'm just trying to understand (for myself) what the level of breakage really is. To require it to be impossible is moving the goalposts. That it has been rejected before should be an indication to not try again. Well, impossible is relative of course. Low breakage => possible, very high breakage => impossible. Something inbetween => grey area. > That it has been rejected before should be an indication to not try again. Well, to be clear: I am not at all proposing to try again!! Making previously valid jumpdests invalid was the argument used to reject it, so any solution proposed needs to fit that bill. Is it a strong enough argument though, to say that something was previously rejected so we need a completely new way? I mean, I have no idea It means we cannot introduce it in a way that changes semantics of previously contracts. Hi everybody, hope you don't mind me posting here.  I'm looking at the recent EOF presentation slides from ACDE.  I'm interested in the argument that immediate values change the interpretation of existing code.  The example given (slides 23/24) is: `0x61E001615B610100EFE05BFFC92A` The argument is that adding `RJUMP` leads to a change in validity of the code.  But, I don't see that (in this particular case) it is true.  Assembly code for the example is:
```
.code
        push 0xe001
        push 0x5b61
        add
        stop
.data
        0xefe05bffc92a
```
My understanding of the Yellow Paper suggests that this code would not be affected by the introduction of `RJUMP` as it does not attempt a branch to the second `JUMPDEST`.  Hence, whether or not its considered a valid Jump Destination does not matter.  *Did I miss something here?*

Anyway, an example like this seems to make more sense to me:
```
.code
   push lab
   jump
   db 0xe0
lab:
   jumpdest
   stop
```
In this case, reinterpreting `0xe0` as an `RJUMP` with a two-byte immediate operand completely changes the meaning of the program.
